posts.title: Counting moss on the north slope
posts.excerpt: Seven years after the first thinning, Tomoe went back to the twelve survey plots with a square frame and a hand lens. The ground is turning green.
posts.content:
In 2019 the floor of plot N4 was bare: dark needles, a little mud, nothing growing under the crowded cedar. This September Tomoe Arai knelt in the same spot with a one-metre square frame and counted eleven kinds of moss and four ferns.

Why moss matters

Moss is the first thing to come back when light reaches the ground. It holds water after rain, keeps the soil from sliding and gives seeds somewhere to land. If the moss is returning, the rest of the forest usually follows.

I used to dread the north plots. Now I need twice as long to count them.

Tomoe Arai, ecologist

The full results go into next spring's impact report. For now: two thirds of the thinned plots are green, and the untouched control plots are still bare.

posts.title: Two hundred cedars thinned, four hundred oaks planted
posts.excerpt: Our biggest work day of the year: forty-four volunteers, three foresters and a very long lunch on the east slope.
posts.content:
It rained in the morning and nobody minded. By nine the minibus had made three trips from the station, and by ten the first cedars marked in August were coming down on the upper terrace.

Light, then oak

The foresters took out roughly one tree in three, choosing the thinnest and the most crowded. Volunteers followed behind, planting two-year-old oaks from the nursery in the new gaps and fixing a tube around each against the deer.

  • 212 cedars thinned and left on the slope
  • 418 oaks and 60 maples planted
  • 44 volunteers, 9 of them for the first time

Thank you to everyone who came, and to the school kitchen for the miso soup.

posts.title: The nursery's best year: four thousand seedlings ready
posts.excerpt: A good acorn year two autumns ago means the greenhouse is full. Here is what is growing, and where it will go.
posts.content:
Two autumns ago the oaks in the valley had a mast year, dropping more acorns than anyone could remember. Our volunteers gathered sacks of them. Now the benches in the greenhouse are full, and the young trees are ready for the slopes.

What is on the benches

  • 2,600 konara oak
  • 800 beech
  • 450 mountain maple
  • 220 alder for the stream banks

They will be planted between November and March, mostly on the north slope where the thinning finished last winter. If you would like to plant one yourself, the work days are open.

posts.title: Forty-two nest boxes, thirty-one families
posts.excerpt: The nest box check is the happiest job of the year. This spring brought a record, and an unexpected pair of owls.
posts.content:
Each box is opened twice a season, quickly and quietly, by two volunteers with a ladder and a notebook. This year thirty-one of the forty-two had been used: tits, flycatchers, a nuthatch, and in box 17, two owl chicks staring back.

We built that box for owls in 2014. It took them twelve years to agree.

Kenji Oda, head forester

Owls need old, open woodland with plenty of mice, which is exactly what the thinning is meant to bring back. We are not claiming credit yet, but we are very pleased.

posts.title: Winter work days: what changes when it snows
posts.excerpt: Winter is our busiest season, not our quietest. Here is how the work days change from December to February, and what to wear.
posts.content:
Trees are planted while they sleep, so winter is when the most happens on the slopes. The days are shorter, and so are ours: we start at nine and are back at the office by one.

What to wear

  • Warm layers, not one thick coat
  • Waterproof boots, a size up for thick socks
  • A hat and spare gloves; ours get wet

When there is deep snow, we swap planting for a slow snowshoe walk with Tomoe to read the tracks. Foxes, hares, deer and, once, a serow.

posts.title: Our 2025 impact report is out
posts.excerpt: What we planted, what it cost, what went wrong and what we will change: the short version, with a link to the full thirty-two pages.
posts.content:
Every spring we publish everything: the numbers, the maps, the accounts and the auditor's letter. This year's report is the longest yet, mostly because the bird survey had so much good news.

The short version

  • 4,120 trees planted, 87% survival after two years
  • 3.4 km of stream cleared and two weirs removed
  • 612 volunteers and nine school classes

We also missed our spring planting target because of the wet weather, and spent more than planned on deer fences. Both are explained in the report, with what we will do differently. Read it on the impact page, and tell us what you think.

posts.title: Trout above the old weir
posts.excerpt: Eight years after the first weir came out of the Sugidani, young trout have been found four kilometres upstream.
posts.content:
The concrete weir at the bend below the school was built in the 1960s to slow the river. It also stopped every fish that tried to swim past it. In 2017 a team of volunteers took it apart by hand, block by block, over six weekends.

This summer's fish count found young trout in the side streams above it for the first time in living memory.

You could hear the river change the day the last block came out.

A volunteer from the 2017 team

Two more weirs are planned for next summer. If you like cold water and heavy lifting, we would love your help.
